# NC Parole Commission PRSPC

> **Educational only, NOT legal advice.** For specific legal matters, consult a licensed North Carolina attorney.

`verified-as-of: 2026-06-22`

## Overview

The **NC Post-Release Supervision and Parole Commission (PRSPC)** is an independent state agency that operates alongside NC DAC. Its dual function reflects NC's two-era sentencing history: (1) traditional discretionary **parole** for persons convicted before October 1, 1994 under Fair Sentencing or earlier laws; and (2) mandatory **post-release supervision (PRS)** conditions for persons sentenced under the 1994 Structured Sentencing Act.[^1]

**Contact:** Parole.Commission@dac.nc.gov | 919-716-3010

## Core Concepts

### 1. Commission Structure (GS 143B-1490)

The Commission has **four members** appointed by the Governor, who also selects the **chairman**. The Commission is an independent agency — not part of DAC administratively.[^1]

A **majority** of the Commission must agree to deny or approve parole for all eligible offenders. This means at least 3 of 4 commissioners must vote to approve a discretionary parole grant.

**Commission Reports** published annually: Medical Release Report, Parole Eligibility Report, MAPP Report — available at https://www.dac.nc.gov/divisions-and-sections/post-release-supervision-and-parole-commission/commission-reports

### 2. The 1994 Divide: Parole vs. Post-Release Supervision

| Aspect | Discretionary Parole | Post-Release Supervision (PRS) |
|--------|---------------------|-------------------------------|
| Who | Convicted BEFORE Oct. 1, 1994 | Convicted AFTER Oct. 1, 1994 (Structured Sentencing) |
| PRSPC role | Decides whether and when to release | Sets conditions only (release is mandatory upon completion of prison term) |
| Duration | Commission-set | GS-defined based on offense class |
| Revocation | Commission initiates | Court revokes |

**Key implication:** For persons sentenced under Structured Sentencing (post-1994), the PRSPC does **not** decide whether they get released — release is mandatory after serving the minimum active sentence. The PRSPC only sets the conditions of supervision for these individuals.[^1]

For pre-1994 Fair Sentencing/Old Sentencing era prisoners, the PRSPC has full discretionary parole authority — deciding if, when, and under what conditions the person is released.

### 3. MAPP — Mutual Agreement Parole Program

MAPP is a **three-way agreement** between:
- The NC Post-Release Supervision and Parole Commission
- NC DAC Prison System
- The individual inmate

**History:** MAPP began in 1975 as a pilot and went statewide in 1976, initially focused on committed youthful offenders and vocational training programs.[^2]

**Eligibility:** MAPP is available **only** for offenders convicted of crimes committed **before October 1, 1994** (pre-Structured Sentencing era). No parole (and thus no MAPP) exists for post-1994 convictions.

**Purpose:** MAPP encourages behavioral change by establishing a parole date contingent on the inmate completing specific educational/vocational/programming milestones, creating a structured path to release.

**Current scope:** Today MAPP serves as a management tool that rewards appropriate behavior, evaluates readiness for release, and prepares the offender for successful reentry.[^2]

### 4. Medical Release Program

NC's Medical Release Program allows the Commission to release terminally ill, permanently and totally disabled, or geriatric inmates who no longer pose a public safety risk.[^3]

**Eligibility criteria:**
- Permanently and totally disabled, terminally ill, OR geriatric
- Incapacitated to the extent they do not pose a risk to public safety
- DAC must first determine the inmate meets medical criteria and refer to Commission

**Ineligible:** Persons convicted of capital felonies, Class A, B1, or B2 felonies, or sex offenses requiring registration are **not eligible** for early medical release.

**Process:**
1. DAC evaluates medical criteria and public safety risk
2. If criteria met, DAC refers case to Commission
3. Commission has 15-20 days to make independent determination
4. Commission votes (majority required)

**Usage statistics (2024):** In 2024 (first full year under expanded 2023 eligibility criteria), the Commission granted medical release to **4 people** out of ~32,000 in the statewide prison population. Since 2019, 67 total medical releases have been granted.[^3]

**Reform context:** A 2025 NC Health News investigation found the program underutilized despite 2023 legislative reforms aimed at expanding access.

### 5. Parole Hearing Process

For discretionary parole (pre-1994 era cases):[^1]
- **Commission review:** Cases are reviewed according to eligibility schedules
- **Staff analysis:** DAC staff prepare case summaries, risk assessments, victim input
- **Commission vote:** Majority (3/4) required to grant parole
- **Conditions set:** If granted, Commission establishes conditions
- **Victim notification:** Victims registered with NC DAC are notified of hearings and decisions
- **Denial:** Commission may deny parole; case is scheduled for future review

### 6. Post-Release Supervision Conditions

For Structured Sentencing offenders (post-1994), the PRSPC sets conditions of PRS, which may include:[^1]
- Report to assigned probation/parole officer
- Remain in assigned county/district
- Maintain lawful employment
- Submit to searches
- Electronic monitoring (for high-risk offenders)
- Sex offender-specific conditions (if applicable — see `nc-sex-offender-supervision`)
- Drug testing and treatment
- No firearms possession

**Duration of PRS** is set by statute based on offense class:
- Class B1-E felonies: 9 months PRS (mandatory)
- Class F-I felonies: May include PRS depending on sentence structure
- Class B1-E with prior record: Up to 5 years PRS for certain violent offenders

### 7. Parole Commission Manual 2024

The official Parole Commission Manual (revised 2024) governs internal Commission operations, standards for parole decisions, conditions, and procedures. Available at: https://files.nc.gov/dac/documents/2024-11/Parole%20Commission%20Manual%20Revised%202024.pdf

## Anti-Patterns / Common Mistakes

- **Assuming PRSPC grants "parole" to post-1994 offenders:** Post-1994 structured sentencing offenders are released mandatorily; PRSPC only sets their supervision conditions.[^1]
- **Confusing MAPP eligibility with all NC parole:** MAPP and discretionary parole apply only to pre-October 1994 convictions.
- **Expecting medical release to be easily obtained:** The program is rarely used — 4 grants in 2024 out of 32,000 prisoners.[^3]
- **Thinking PRS revocation goes through PRSPC:** PRS violations for post-1994 offenders are handled in court (criminal court revocation), not by the Commission alone.
